scenes.spec: quiet suburban street, morning, car backing out of a driveway
scenes.narration: Six-thirty in the morning. You back out of the driveway, touch the brakes, and your car announces you to the entire neighborhood — a squeal you can feel in your teeth. Here's the strange part: sometimes that squeak means absolutely nothing. And sometimes it's your brakes *deliberately* making that noise — on purpose, by design — to tell you something. By the end of this video you'll know how to tell the difference.

scenes.spec: channel card — "Why Is My Car Doing That?"

scenes.narration: Squeaks come in flavors, and the flavor is the diagnosis. Ask yourself three questions.

scenes.spec: three-way split — "When does it squeak?" / "Cold or warm?" / "Does it stop when you brake harder?"
scenes.narration: **One: when?** A squeal *only while braking* is a brake noise. A squeal that runs constantly while driving and *disappears* when you press the pedal — that's a very specific message, and we'll get to it, because it's the one your brakes make on purpose. **Two: cold or warm?** A squeak on the first few stops of a cold, damp morning that vanishes once everything warms up is usually the most innocent noise a car can make. **Three: pressure.** Light-pedal squeal that goes quiet when you press harder points one direction; a grind or growl that gets *worse* with pressure points somewhere much more expensive.

scenes.section: THE MECHANISM — WHY BRAKES SING AT ALL
scenes.spec: front corner assembly — the ep-1 3D scene, camera pushing to the pad/rotor contact
scenes.narration: Quick physics, because it makes everything else obvious. A brake squeal is a vibration — the pad, caliper, and rotor form a system that can resonate like a violin string when the pad slides across the disc. At a few thousand vibrations per second, steel-on-friction-material sings in exactly the frequency band human ears hate most. [TECH CONFIRM — anything you'd add about which components you find actually resonating most often?] The engineering question is never "why is it vibrating" — everything vibrates. It's "what changed, so that the vibration stopped being damped?"

scenes.section: CAUSE #1 — SURFACE RUST AFTER RAIN OR A CAR WASH (most common, most innocent)
scenes.spec: rotor surface strip from ep 1, thin orange film building overnight, first stops scrubbing it clean
scenes.narration: Steel rotors rust *overnight*. A humid night, rain, a car wash before parking — by morning there's an invisible orange film on the discs. The first few stops scrub it off, and that scrubbing is your morning squeal. Gone in half a mile. This is the noise that means nothing. If your squeak only shows up cold and damp and always fades — you can stop watching this video. [TECH CONFIRM — agree that's dischargeable advice, or do you want a caveat here?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #2 — THE WEAR INDICATOR (the squeal that's on purpose)
scenes.spec: pad side-view — friction material wearing down toward a small steel tab, tab touching rotor
scenes.narration: Inside most brake pads is a little steel tab called a **wear indicator**, set at the legal-minimum pad thickness. When the friction material wears down to it, the tab drags on the rotor and produces a constant, high squeal while you drive — that *stops* when you press the pedal, because braking pressure changes the contact. That pattern — sings while cruising, silent while braking — is your car saying: **pads are done, book the appointment.** Not an emergency today. An emergency if you ignore it for a month, because after the squealer comes the grinding — and grinding means the pad backing plate is eating your rotor. [TECH CONFIRM — typical time/miles between "squealer starts" and "metal on metal" in your experience?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #3 — GLAZED PADS OR CHEAP PADS
scenes.spec: pad magnified — surface shiny and crystallized vs healthy matte surface
scenes.narration: Pads that got cooked — a mountain descent, a panic stop, riding the brakes — can **glaze**: the friction surface crystallizes into a hard, shiny layer that squeals like chalk on a board and, worse, *grips less*. Budget pads with high metal content do the same thing from day one. Glazing often shows up WITH a change in pedal feel — takes more push to stop the same way. [TECH CONFIRM — your shop's take on economy vs mid-tier pads; do you see glazing more on a specific brand/type?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #4 — MISSING HARDWARE: SHIMS, CLIPS, AND LUBE
scenes.spec: exploded pad assembly — shim, abutment clips, slide points highlighted
scenes.narration: Between the pad and caliper piston there's supposed to be a **shim** — a thin damper whose whole job is killing the vibration we talked about. Pads sit in **abutment clips**, and their contact points get a dab of brake grease at install. A rushed brake job that skips the shims, reuses old rusty clips, or skips the lube produces a brand-new brake that squeals worse than the old one. If your squeak started *right after* a brake job — this is the prime suspect, and it's a warranty-of-workmanship conversation, not a new-parts conversation. [TECH CONFIRM — how often do squeak complaints trace to missing/skipped hardware from a previous shop?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #5 — STICKING CALIPER OR RUSTY SLIDE PINS
scenes.spec: caliper cross-section from ep 1 — seized slide pin, pad dragging lightly
scenes.narration: The same sticking caliper from our brake-shake episode can whistle instead of shake: a lightly-dragging pad hums or squeals at speed, brake or no brake, often with one wheel running hot and fuel economy dipping. Squeal plus pull to one side, or squeal plus a hot wheel — caliper service, this week.

scenes.narration: Match the fix to the flavor: soon, priced as routine maintenance — the cheapest brake job you'll ever get is the one before the grinding starts. resurface or replacement so the fresh pads bed into a clean surface. dragging cooked. scenes.spec: three-tier verdict card — "Ignore it" / "Book it" / "This week"
scenes.narration: **Ignore it:** cold-morning squeal that fades with the first few stops. The one noise on this channel you're allowed to do nothing about. **Book it:** the constant cruise-squeal that quiets under braking — the wear indicator. You have some runway, and none to waste. **This week:** squeal with a hot wheel, a pull, pedal-feel changes — or any squeal that's become a **grind**. Grinding is metal on metal; every mile is money. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the tiers or move a boundary]

So: damp-morning squeals are rust scrubbing itself off, a cruise-squeal that stops when you brake is your pads' built-in appointment reminder, and a squeal that arrived with a hot wheel or a pull is a caliper waving for help. Your brakes talk. Now you speak the language. Next time: your brake pedal is pulsing under your foot — and the villain is a rotor that isn't the same thickness everywhere. That one's stranger than it sounds.
